question: Why do nurses need to assist some patients with feeding?

options.A: To ensure adequate nutrition for patients who cannot feed themselves
options.B: To completely eliminate the risk of choking during every meal
options.C: To speed up meal times in busy hospital wards
options.D: To test the patient's swallowing reflexes before discharge

explanation: You've got this! Assisted feeding is simply stepping in to help patients who aren't able to eat on their own yet, making sure they get the strength they need. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h1)

question: A stroke patient is struggling to hold a spoon because of weak arms. What should you do?

options.A: Initiate assisted feeding to ensure the patient gets enough food
options.B: Insist the patient feed themselves to encourage independence
options.C: Withhold meals until the patient regains full arm strength
options.D: Switch the patient immediately to total parenteral nutrition

explanation: Great clinical instinct! When weakness gets in the way of holding utensils safely, stepping in with assisted feeding keeps your patient nourished and cared for. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h1)

question: What is a quick, thoughtful step to take before bringing a food tray to a patient's bed?

options.A: Lock the room door so visitors do not interrupt the meal
options.B: Remove unpleasant items like bedpans or trash from sight
options.C: Brush the patient's teeth with harsh antiseptic mouthwash
options.D: Force the patient to walk around the room to build an appetite

explanation: Nobody wants to eat next to a bedpan! Clearing away bad sights and smells makes mealtime much more appetizing and pleasant. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h2)

question: Why must you always check the meal tray against the patient's diet ticket before feeding?

options.A: To calculate the exact financial cost of the hospital meal
options.B: To check if the kitchen included extra dessert for the nurse
options.C: To measure the exact weight of the food for hospital records
options.D: To confirm the correct food consistency and dietary restrictions

explanation: Spot-checking the diet ticket is a key safety habit. It ensures your patient gets the right textures—like pureed foods when needed—preventing dangerous mix-ups. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h2)

question: What is the best position to place a patient in before you start feeding them?

options.A: Trendelenburg position with feet elevated higher than the head
options.B: High Fowler's position or 90 degrees upright in a chair
options.C: Semi-Fowler's position at a gentle 30-degree angle
options.D: Flat on the back with a small pillow under the neck

explanation: Sitting upright uses gravity to help food go down smoothly and, most importantly, keeps the airway safe from choking. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h3)

question: Why should a patient stay sitting upright for about 30 minutes after eating?

options.A: To allow the nurse enough time to clear the bedside table
options.B: To prevent food reflux and reduce the risk of aspiration
options.C: To encourage the patient to fall into a deep sleep
options.D: To help the digestive enzymes break down fats faster

explanation: Staying upright gives the stomach a head start on digesting, stopping food or acid from creeping back up into the throat. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h3)

question: How much food should you put on the spoon when feeding an adult patient?

options.D: Packed tightly to the very top

explanation: Smaller spoonfuls are much easier and safer for the patient to chew and swallow without getting overwhelmed. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h4)

question: Your patient keeps trying to talk and laugh with food in their mouth. What should you do?

options.A: Keep pushing the next spoonful of food into the mouth quickly
options.B: Scold the patient firmly for bad table manners
options.C: Ask the patient to finish chewing and swallowing before speaking
options.D: Remove the food tray immediately and skip the meal

explanation: Friendly reminders work best! Gently asking them to swallow first keeps them safe from choking while keeping the mood warm. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h4)

question: What is a common sign of 'silent aspiration' in someone with swallowing difficulties?

options.A: Red flushing of the cheeks and forehead
options.B: A wet, gurgling voice sound after swallowing
options.C: Excessive sweating on the palms of the hands
options.D: A sudden spike in blood pressure

explanation: That wet or gurgling sound is a classic red flag! It often means a little bit of food or liquid slipped past the vocal cords without triggering a cough. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h5)

question: Why are finger foods so helpful for patients with advanced dementia during meals?

options.A: It prevents the patient from spilling liquids on their hospital gown
options.B: It guarantees the patient will eat three full meals every single day
options.C: It promotes independence and makes eating easier for confused patients
options.D: It eliminates the need for any nursing staff supervision

explanation: Spot on! When handling cutlery gets confusing, finger foods let patients feed themselves and hold onto their dignity. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h5)

question: What key details should you document after helping a patient with a meal?

options.A: The approximate percentage of food eaten and fluid intake
options.B: The total financial cost of the hospital meal ingredients
options.C: The exact brand name of the food served on the tray
options.D: The names of all family members who visited during lunch

explanation: Tracking how much they actually ate and drank helps the whole care team monitor their recovery and hydration. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h6)

question: Why is oral care important right after a patient finishes a meal?

options.A: To remove leftover food particles and prevent bacterial growth
options.B: To stimulate the salivary glands to produce extra digestive acid
options.C: To cool down the patient's mouth temperature after warm food
options.D: To check if the patient's tooth enamel is strong enough

explanation: Cleaning the mouth clears away trapped food crumbs, keeping teeth healthy and preventing bacteria from heading down into the airway later. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h6)
